text:
# termina as the terminal backend

mina's terminal layer uses termina (0.3.x), the low-level VT crate that Helix itself adopted for Unix rendering and events (PR #13307, merged 2025-08), instead of the more established crossterm or the ratatui widget framework. termina provides what a modal editor needs — kitty keyboard protocol, bracketed paste, synchronized output, resize, and a tokio-ready event stream — while keeping the escape-code-level control that Helix-style custom rendering requires. mina owns the cell buffer and frame diff itself, exactly as Helix does. If termina's pre-1.0 API proves unstable, crossterm is the drop-in fallback (it is what Helix ran before).

text:
# Daemon + client split from day one

mina runs as a local daemon from v1: a persistent daemon process owns the editor state (documents, histories, LSP clients) and serves it over a local IPC channel, while the terminal UI, CLI, and agents connect as Clients that send Commands and receive state. Modeled on Hunk's session daemon (`hunk daemon serve` + `hunk session …`). The alternative — a single in-process editor with the process boundary retrofitted later — was rejected: the daemon is the product's core (agent-driven editing, warm LSP, fast attach), and retrofitting a process boundary after the fact is the expensive path. Commands-as-data and a shared protocol crate make the boundary real from the start.

text:
# Request/response state-snapshot IPC, no push channel

mina's IPC is request/response only: a Client sends a Command and the Daemon replies with a full StateSnapshot (document text, selection, mode, viewport, diagnostics), framed as NDJSON over a local unix socket. There is no server-initiated push or subscription channel in v1 — the TUI redraws after each command anyway, and LSP-derived state (Diagnostics) is carried in the next snapshot. Rejected for now: push/event channels (additive later if a client must react while idle), diffed/partial snapshots (deferred until large-file profiling demands), binary serialization (NDJSON kept for debuggability — agents can read the wire).

text:
# Undo groups close on leaving Insert and on client disconnect

An UndoGroup — a set of Transactions reverted by a single undo — spans exactly one Insert session: it opens when the editor enters Insert mode and closes when it leaves Insert (to Normal or Select), or when the owning Client disconnects while in Insert (which also returns the editor to Normal). The alternative — closing only on Insert→Normal — leaves the group open through Select transitions and, worse, through client churn: because the daemon and its History are persistent (ADR-0005), an unclosed group merges edits from different sessions into one undo unit, silently destroying undo granularity (edits from a previous session vanish on a single undo). Connection-scoped groups were rejected for v1 — under the effectively-one-client model a daemon-side boundary is sufficient; a future multi-client model can revisit by making group scope explicit in the protocol.

text:
# Open rejects non-regular and oversized files

mina refuses to open paths that are not regular files (directories, devices such as /dev/zero, FIFOs) and files larger than 16 MiB, reporting "file too large" / "cannot open" in the snapshot status without touching editor state. The daemon checks metadata (is_file + size) before reading. Rationale: v1's full-snapshot-per-command IPC and full-text LSP sync (ADR-0006) make multi-hundred-MiB files unusable regardless of the cap, and an unbounded read is an OOM and hang vector — /dev/zero reads forever, a FIFO blocks forever, a growing log balloons memory. The cap is a plain constant, revisited when diffed snapshots (a v1 non-goal) land and large-file mode becomes viable. Command lines are similarly bounded (1 MiB) so a newline-less stream cannot grow the daemon's read buffer without limit.

text:
# LSP runs outside the daemon lock and respawns on the next Open

The LspSession lives behind its own mutex (`Arc<Mutex<LspSession>>`) inside the Daemon. Spawning, `initialize`, `didOpen`, and `didChange` are awaited outside the daemon lock, each bounded by a timeout (2s writes, 10s requests); diagnostic drains use `try_lock` so a busy server never blocks command processing. Rationale: v1's primary use is agent-driven editing while a human TUI attaches — a slow or hung language server must stall the editing pipeline, not every client. Previously the daemon lock was held across LSP I/O, so one hung rust-analyzer froze all sessions (and, with no write timeout, permanently). If the server dies — detected via the notification channel closing when the reader task hits EOF — edits stop syncing silently (no wasted timeout waits) and the session respawns on the next .rs Open (re-`initialize` + `didOpen` from scratch). No respawn loop is possible because respawn only happens on Open, and a broken server surfaces its `initialize` failure in the snapshot status.

Previously the daemon lock was held across LSP I/O, so one hung rust-analyzer froze all sessions (and, with no write timeout, permanently). If the server dies — detected via the notification channel closing when the reader task hits EOF — edits stop syncing silently (no wasted timeout waits) and the session respawns on the next .rs Open (re-`initialize` + `didOpen` from scratch). No respawn loop is possible because respawn only happens on Open, and a broken server surfaces its `initialize` failure in the snapshot status.

# Clean-room implementation modeled on Helix

mina is modeled on the Helix editor (MPL-2.0), but every line of implementation is written from scratch. We study Helix's concepts and type design — anchor/head ranges, OT-style transactions, workspace crate layout — and reimplement them in our own code; we never copy source files. This keeps mina free of MPL-2.0's file-level obligations and forces us to actually understand the design we borrow.

# Functional core: Selection lives outside Document

The editing core is functional: primitives transform state instead of mutating it — `(document, selection) → (new_document, new_selection)`. A Document owns its text; the active Selection is not stored on it, it is passed into each operation. This mirrors Helix's decision to keep selections per-View (one document can be shown in several splits). Adopting it from day one avoids an API rewrite when views arrive.
